steps.title: The right number of children
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 149 words

Ask six parents what the ideal number is and you will get six answers, each of which happens to be the number they have.

The parent of one says that if she had a second, she would divide her time, money and energy in half, and that the stereotype about only children being spoilt and lonely is not supported. The parent of four says the idea of having fewer is as unthinkable as having fewer arms.

One argues that if everybody in rich countries had fewer children, the pressure on the world's resources would fall. Another makes the case for none at all: if she had had children, she would not have had the life she has.

The one who says she did not plan three had twins, and now believes three is ideal: if two of the siblings fall out, there is always a third to turn to.

steps.title: What does the writer notice about the six answers?
options: Each parent names the number they happen to have.
None of them gives a number.
steps.answer: Each parent names the number they happen to have.
steps.why: The observation is in the first sentence, and everything after it is the evidence.

steps.title: What a sibling is actually for
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 147 words

The research on siblings is more interesting than the arguments about numbers. Only children are not, on average, more spoilt, more lonely or less able to make friends. That result has been reproduced for forty years and almost nobody believes it.

What siblings do provide is practice. A brother or a sister is the first person you are mean to who does not stop loving you, the first person you have to stand up to, and the first person who tells you, without any tact at all, what other people are too polite to say.

If I had grown up without my sister, I would probably be a more agreeable person and a considerably worse judge of character. She told me at nine that I was showing off. Nobody outside the family would have said it, and if she had not, I would have gone on doing it for years.

steps.title: Second and third conditional
steps.html:
Two conditionals, one for the present and one for the past — and the mixed form between them.

The second conditional is for an unreal present or future: if + past simple, would + infinitive. If she had a second child, she would divide her time in half. She does not have one; this is imagined.

The past tense does not mean past time. It marks distance from reality — the same trick as in I wouldn't be surprised if it happened from Lesson 20.

The third conditional is for an unreal past: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. If she had had children, she would not have had the life she has. It is finished; nothing can change it.

The mixed conditional joins the two: a past condition with a present result. If I had grown up without my sister, I would probably be a worse judge of character. The growing up is past; the being is now.

You can replace would with could or might to soften the claim: she might have said it, history could have been very different.

Two things to avoid. Never put would in the if clause: if I would have known. And were is used for all persons in the formal second conditional: if I were you.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts and around them.

If she had a second, she would divide her time in half.
Second: unreal present.

If everybody had fewer children, the pressure would fall.
Second, about the world now.

If she had had children, she would not have had this life.
Third: finished, unchangeable.

If I had grown up without my sister, I would probably be more agreeable.
Mixed: past cause, present result.

If she had not, I would have gone on doing it for years.
Third, with the condition reduced to two words.

Nobody outside the family would have said it.
Third conditional result with no if clause at all.

If two of them fall out, there is always a third.
First conditional — this one is real.

I wouldn't be surprised if it happened.
Second, from Lesson 20.

History could have been very different.
Could softens the third conditional.

She might have told me anyway.
Might softens it further.

If I were you, I'd wait.
Were for all persons in the formal form.

If I would have known…
Would never goes in the if clause.

steps.title: Second, third, or mixed
steps.html:
1. The facts: you grew up with a sister. You are, now, a good judge of character.
  2. To imagine a different present: If I had a sister, I would understand people better. Second conditional — but this is false here, because you do have one.
  3. To imagine a different past: If I had grown up without her, I would have learned it later. Third conditional: both halves in the past.
  4. To imagine a past cause with a present result: If I had grown up without her, I would be a worse judge of character now. Mixed — and this is the sentence the text actually uses.
  5. Check the two rules. No would after if. And the past perfect in the if clause is what makes it past, not the would have.

steps.title: You are going to write about a person in your family.

options.label: Somebody who told you something nobody else would

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least one second conditional, one third conditional and one mixed conditional.
steps.html:
• Open with a third conditional about who you would have been.
  • Describe one specific thing that person did or said.
  • Use a mixed conditional for how you would be now.
  • Close with a second conditional about the present.

Useful language

  • If I had grown up without … , I would …
  • Nobody outside the family would have said it.
  • If she hadn't … , I would probably still be …
  • I take after … , which is why …
  • It turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
  • If I were doing it again, I would …
steps.modelHtml:
My brother, four years older

If I had been an only child I would have been intolerable. I say that with some confidence, because I was intolerable for the first eight years, and then he told me so.

He was not being kind. He was eleven and I had taken something of his. But nobody outside the family would have said it in those words, and if he had not, I would probably still be waiting for somebody to explain why people found me tiring.

We have never been close in the way people mean by close. We speak about four times a year. If I needed something serious, though, I would call him before anybody else, and I know without asking that it works the same way in the other direction.

That turns out to be what a sibling is: not company, but a person you can call.
